title: Thirty days, then a year
hookLine: mourning eases after thirty days; Kaddish continues for a parent

cards: The last chapter of the Torah. Moses climbs a mountain, looks out over the land he will never enter, and dies there. Below, the people grieve, and the text gives their grief a length.

In the old Jewish Publication Society translation, the children of Israel "wept for Moses in the plains of Moab thirty days". Then the days of weeping end. The very next line turns to Joshua, and the people listen to him.
They don't forget Moses. They can't. But after thirty days, they get up and walk forward.

teach.b: Shloshim means thirty. Turn it four ways. First, the text.
Moses is mourned for thirty days, and so, the book of Numbers says, is his brother Aaron. Jewish law reads those thirty days as a pattern for every mourner. Second, the steps.
Shiva comes first, the low chair and the open door. When it ends, in some communities, the mourners walk together around the block, stepping back into the street for the first time.
Through the rest of the thirty days they return to work and errands but hold back from parties and celebrations, and some don't cut their hair. Life starts again, quietly. Third, a parent.

For other close relatives, formal mourning ends at thirty days. For a father or a mother, tradition keeps it going through much of the year, and the child says the mourner's Kaddish with a congregation, day after day.
A parent, the tradition seems to say, takes longer to set down. Fourth, the shape of it.

Grief here isn't a switch that turns off on a date. It's a set of doors, each a little wider than the last: the grave, the week, the month, the year. Nobody expects you to come through the first door already healed.
They only expect you to keep coming, slowly, and they keep a place for you while you do.

how: After shiva, Jewish mourners keep shloshim, the thirty days from the burial: they return to work but avoid celebrations; for a parent the mourning continues through much of the year, with the mourner's Kaddish said in synagogue.

practice: Bring to mind something that changed for you lately, or still feels raw: a loss, a move, an ending.

Ask gently where you are on the steps, still on the low chair, out walking around the block, back at work but not at the party yet, and know there's no wrong answer; if you pray, bring it into your prayer.
And if a loss you're carrying ever feels like too much, please reach out: in the US you can call or text 988, or call local emergency help.

wordCard.voice: Shloshim. Thirty: the month after a death, when mourners return to life slowly, and for a parent the mourning goes on. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: thirty, the first month of mourning.

carryVoice: Your line: slowly back. Grief keeps its own calendar, and that is allowed. Until tomorrow.
